before: Blind spot accidents are among the most preventable yet frequently occurring crashes on roads throughout Georgia and South Carolina. When a driver fails to check a blind spot before changing lanes, merging, or turning, the results can be devastating — from sideswipe collisions on the interstate to fatal crashes involving motorcyclists and pedestrians. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), lane-change crashes account for approximately 240,000 accidents per year nationwide, and a significant percentage of those involve blind spot failures.
after: Blind spot accidents are among the most preventable yet frequently occurring crashes on roads throughout Georgia and South Carolina. When a driver fails to check a blind spot before changing lanes, merging, or turning, the results can be devastating — from sideswipe collisions on the interstate to fatal crashes involving motorcyclists and pedestrians. According to the most detailed lane-change study by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), two-vehicle lane-change crashes numbered about 539,000 in 1999 — roughly 9 percent of all police-reported crashes that year.

before: A blind spot is an area around a vehicle that the driver cannot see through side mirrors, rearview mirrors, or direct line of sight. Every vehicle has blind spots, though their size and location vary depending on the type of vehicle. For a standard passenger car, blind spots typically exist on both sides of the vehicle just behind the driver's peripheral vision. For larger vehicles like commercial trucks and SUVs, blind spots can extend several car lengths on all four sides.
after: A blind spot is an area around a vehicle that the driver cannot see through side mirrors, rearview mirrors, or direct line of sight. Every vehicle has blind spots, though their size and location vary depending on the type of vehicle. For a standard passenger car, blind spots typically exist on both sides of the vehicle just behind the driver's peripheral vision. SUVs and pickups have larger rear and side blind zones than cars, and around commercial trucks, blind spots can extend several car lengths on all four sides.

before: The most common blind spot accident occurs when a driver changes lanes without seeing a vehicle in the adjacent lane. The result is typically a sideswipe collision that can push either vehicle into a guardrail, median, or other traffic. On Georgia interstates like I-95, I-16, and I-26 in South Carolina, high-speed sideswipes can lead to multi-vehicle pileups.

before: Most drivers position their side mirrors so they can see the rear fender of their own vehicle. Instead, angle each side mirror outward until you can barely see your vehicle's side. This "BGE method" (named after the Society of Automotive Engineers study that popularized it) dramatically reduces blind spots by creating a seamless field of view from your rearview mirror to your side mirrors to your peripheral vision.
after: Most drivers position their side mirrors so they can see the rear fender of their own vehicle. Instead, lean your head against the driver's window and set the left mirror so you can just see the side of your car, then lean to the center of the car and do the same with the right mirror; from your normal seat, your car should disappear from both side mirrors. This Blindzone and Glare Elimination (BGE) setting, described in a 1995 Society of Automotive Engineers paper, dramatically reduces blind spots by creating a seamless field of view from your rearview mirror to your side mirrors to your peripheral vision.

before: Signaling your intention to change lanes gives other drivers time to react, flash their lights, or honk to alert you of their presence. In both Georgia and South Carolina, failing to use turn signals before a lane change is a traffic violation.
after: Signaling your intention to change lanes gives other drivers time to react, flash their lights, or honk to alert you of their presence. In both Georgia and South Carolina, failing to use turn signals before a lane change is a traffic violation whenever another driver could be affected.

before: Under O.C.G.A. § 40-6-123, Georgia law requires that a driver changing lanes must first ascertain that the movement can be made safely. A driver who causes a collision by changing lanes without checking their blind spot has violated this statute and can be found negligent. Georgia follows a modified comparative fault rule — you can recover damages as long as you are less than 50% at fault for the accident (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). The statute of limitations for personal injury claims in Georgia is 2 years from the date of the accident (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33).
after: Under O.C.G.A. § 40-6-48(1), a Georgia driver may not leave a lane until he or she has first ascertained that the move can be made safely, and O.C.G.A. § 40-6-123 requires an appropriate and timely signal. A driver who causes a collision by changing lanes without checking their blind spot has violated these statutes and can be found negligent. Georgia follows a modified comparative fault rule — you can recover damages as long as you are less than 50% at fault for the accident (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). The statute of limitations for personal injury claims in Georgia is 2 years from the date of the accident (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33).

before: South Carolina law similarly requires drivers to ensure lane changes can be made safely under S.C. Code § 56-5-2150. Drivers must not move from their lane until they have determined that it is safe to do so. South Carolina also follows a modified comparative fault system — you can recover damages if you are less than 51% at fault. The statute of limitations for personal injury claims in South Carolina is 3 years from the date of the accident (S.C. Code § 15-3-530).
after: South Carolina law similarly requires drivers to ensure lane changes can be made safely under S.C. Code § 56-5-2150, which also requires a signal for at least the last 100 feet. Drivers must not move from their lane until they have determined that it is safe to do so (S.C. Code § 56-5-1900(a)). South Carolina also follows a modified comparative fault system — you can recover damages if you are less than 51% at fault. The statute of limitations for personal injury claims in South Carolina is 3 years from the date of the accident (S.C. Code § 15-3-530).

before:
• Police report: The responding officer's report often notes whether a driver was cited for an unsafe lane change or failure to yield.
  • Witness testimony: Other drivers or passengers who saw the lane change can confirm that the at-fault driver did not check their blind spot or signal.
  • Dashcam and traffic camera footage: Video evidence showing the lane change in real time is among the most compelling evidence in these cases.
  • Vehicle damage patterns: The location and angle of damage on both vehicles can help accident reconstructionists determine how the collision occurred and who was at fault.
  • Electronic data recorders (EDR): Modern vehicles record speed, braking, and steering data that can reveal whether the at-fault driver took any evasive action before the crash.

In cases involving commercial trucks, additional evidence may include the truck's side-mirror adjustment records, blind spot monitoring system data, and the trucking company's driver training records.
after:
• Police report: The responding officer's report often notes whether a driver was cited for an unsafe lane change or failure to yield. A citation alone does not prove fault — South Carolina bars evidence of a traffic conviction in a civil case (S.C. Code § 56-5-6160) — but in either state a guilty plea to the ticket can be used as an admission.
  • Witness testimony: Other drivers or passengers who saw the lane change can confirm that the at-fault driver did not check their blind spot or signal.
  • Dashcam and traffic camera footage: Video evidence showing the lane change in real time is among the most compelling evidence in these cases.
  • Vehicle damage patterns: The location and angle of damage on both vehicles can help accident reconstructionists determine how the collision occurred and who was at fault.
  • Electronic data recorders (EDR): Most modern vehicles have an event data recorder that captures speed, accelerator and brake use — and in many vehicles steering input — in the seconds before a crash (49 C.F.R. § 563.7), data that can reveal whether the at-fault driver took any evasive action before the crash.

In cases involving commercial trucks, additional evidence may include the truck's mirror equipment and inspection reports, any camera or blind-spot warning system data, and the driver's qualification file and hours-of-service records.

before:
In cases involving extreme recklessness — such as a driver who was texting while making a blind lane change — Georgia allows punitive damages under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1 to punish the wrongdoer. South Carolina also permits punitive damages in cases of willful, wanton, or reckless conduct.

If a blind spot accident results in a fatality, the victim's family may pursue a wrongful death claim to recover funeral expenses, loss of companionship, and other damages.
after:
When a driver's conduct shows willful misconduct or the conscious indifference to consequences Georgia requires — proven by clear and convincing evidence — punitive damages are available under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1; negligence, even gross negligence, is not enough (Colonial Pipeline Co. v. Brown). Georgia generally caps them at $250,000 unless the driver intended harm or was impaired by alcohol or drugs. South Carolina also permits punitive damages for willful, wanton, or reckless conduct proven by clear and convincing evidence, capped at the greater of three times compensatory damages or $500,000 (indexed to $739,245 for 2026), with no cap for intentional harm, a related felony conviction, or impairment (S.C. Code § 15-32-530).

If a blind spot accident results in a fatality, the victim's family may pursue a wrongful death claim — in Georgia for the full value of the deceased person's life, with funeral and medical expenses recovered through a separate estate claim (O.C.G.A. § 51-4-5(b)); in South Carolina for the family's financial and emotional losses, including loss of companionship.

before: Blind spot accidents cause thousands of injuries annually on Georgia and South Carolina roads, particularly affecting motorcyclists, bicyclists, and pedestrians. Proper mirror adjustment, shoulder checks, and defensive driving significantly reduce risk. Georgia requires safe lane changes under O.C.G.A. § 40-6-123, with a 2-year filing deadline (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). South Carolina imposes similar duties under S.C. Code § 56-5-2150, with a 3-year deadline (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Both states apply modified comparative fault rules.
after: Lane-change crashes number in the hundreds of thousands nationally each year (NHTSA), and blind spot crashes hit motorcyclists, bicyclists, and pedestrians hardest. Proper mirror adjustment, shoulder checks, and defensive driving significantly reduce risk. Georgia requires safe, signaled lane changes under O.C.G.A. §§ 40-6-48 and 40-6-123, with a 2-year filing deadline (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). South Carolina imposes similar duties under S.C. Code §§ 56-5-1900 and 56-5-2150, including a signal for at least the last 100 feet, with a 3-year deadline (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Both states apply modified comparative fault rules.

before: Motorcyclists, bicyclists, and pedestrians face the highest risk because their smaller profiles make them easier to miss. Drivers of compact cars traveling alongside large trucks or SUVs are also at elevated risk due to the larger vehicles extensive blind zones.
after: Motorcyclists, bicyclists, and pedestrians face the highest risk because their smaller profiles make them easier to miss. Drivers of compact cars traveling alongside large trucks or SUVs are also at elevated risk due to the larger vehicles' extensive blind zones.

before: Angle your side mirrors outward until you can barely see your own vehicle, perform shoulder checks before every lane change, use turn signals early, and avoid lingering in other vehicles blind spots. Modern blind spot monitoring systems can supplement but should not replace these habits.
after: Lean your head toward each window and set that side mirror so you can just see your own car — from your normal seat it will then disappear from view — perform shoulder checks before every lane change, use turn signals early, and avoid lingering in other vehicles' blind spots. This is the Blindzone and Glare Elimination (BGE) setting described in a 1995 Society of Automotive Engineers paper. Modern blind spot monitoring systems can supplement but should not replace these habits.
